BG	Chem	(Pty)	Ltd	is	a	business	that	produces,	sanitisers,	disinfectants	and	Personal		
Protective	Equipment	(PPE).		It	also	helps	with	disinfecting	houses,	shops	and	schools.
At	first,	the	business	used	a	batch	production	method.		 Towards	the	end	of	2020,	the		
business	lost	its	market	share.		As	BG	Chem	(Pty)	Ltd	could	not	keep	up	with	demand,	 	
local	customers	started	buying	disinfectants	and	PPE	from	its	rivals.		The	owners	of	BG	
Chem	(Pty)	Ltd	decided	to	purchase	modern	machinery	that	can	be	used	to	produce	disin-
fectants	and	PPEs	in	large	quantities.
At	the	beginning	of	2021,	the	owners	thought	of	expanding	to	benefit	from	cost	advantages.	 	
They	decided	to	convert	the	business	into	a	Private	Limited	Company.
Workers	 decided	 to	 communicate	 their	 concerns	 about	 a	 range	 of	 problems	 to	 the		
management.	 	However,	 every	 time	 they	 tried	 to	 raise	 these	 problems,	 employers		
promised	it	would	be	discussed,	with	feedback	provided	through	emails	-	this	never		
happened.		Some	workers	also	felt	it	was	not	a	good	idea	for	the	management	to	respond	
via	email	as	most	of	them	would	end	up	not	getting	this	information.		The	management	
decided	to	involve	the	workers	through	quality	circles	and	a	democratic	style	of	leadership	
as	ways	to	improve	worker	participation.
Discussions	between	managers	and	trade	unions	broke	down.		The	trade	union	decided	to	
take	industrial	action.

Billy’s Tin Factory (BTF)
Billy	decided	to	start	his	own	factory,	producing	tins	used	for	seafood.		Billy’s	Tin	Factory	
(BTF)	sells	a	variety	of	seafood	tins	for	tung,	mackerel	and	sardines.		The	numbers	of		
orders	from	fish	factories	increased	because	of	a	good	reputation.		
With	his	detailed	business	plan,	he	managed	to	get	a	loan	for	a	much	bigger	premises	and	
an	investment	in	more	modern	machinery	to	produce	seafood	tins.		He	needs	to	employ	
more	semi-skilled	and	unskilled	factory	workers.
Currently	BTF	is	producing	a	single	product	at	a	time.		 Due	to	the	increase	in	orders		
received,	BTF	will	need	to	produce	a	large	quantity	of	one	type	of	tin	followed	by	a	large	
quantity	of	another	type	of	tin.
Following	 government	 regulations	 regarding	 business	 activity	 and	 considering	 that		
Namibia	 is	 a	 member	 of	 SADC,	 Billy	 decided	 to	 export	 seafood	 tins	 within	 SADC		
countries.
Billy	experienced	problems	with	his	employees	who	felt	that	Billy	just	makes	his	own		
decisions	without	consulting	them.		The	employees	were	unhappy	and	a	disagreement		
occurred	between	Billy	and	his	employees.		As	some	workers	were	members	of	a	trade	
union,	they	took	their	grievances	to	the	union.
Billy	has	decided	to	franchise	his	business	idea,	brand	name,	promotional	logos	and	trad-
ing	methods.

6144/2/23
Nam Charcoal  
Juan	and	Rudi	started	a	partnership	five	years	ago,	Nam	Charcoal,	a	business	that		
produces	charcoal	for	the	local	market.		Their	business	is	situated	in	the	north	of	Namibia.	
The	business	expanded	quickly	and	they	decided	to	relocate	the	main	office	and	some	
production	to	Botswana,	because	they	export	6	000	ton	of	charcoal	to	Botswana	each	year.	 	
Resources	are	easily	available	in	Botswana	and	no	minimum	wage	is	paid	to	workers.	
The	expansion	of	the	business	changed	the	organisational	structure	of	the	partnership.	 	
They	needed	to	appoint	area	managers	for	each	country	as	well	as	a	financial	manager,	a	
marketing	manager,	a	production	manager	and	more	workers	in	the	production	department	
for	the	expanded	business.		The	partners	borrowed	money	from	a	local	Namibian	bank	to	
finance	the	expansion.
Juan	and	Rudi	asked	their	legal	advisor	for	advice	on	whether	they	should	change	to	a	close		
corporation.		He	discussed	the	pros	and	cons	of	each	form	of	business	ownership	with	
them.
Juan	and	Rudi	know	that	with	the	expansion	to	Botswana	they	must	consider	their	pricing	
strategy	for	charcoal	in	Botswana.		The	market	is	very	competitive	in	Botswana	for	selling	
charcoal.		The	Namibian	government	recently	announced	a	minimum	wage	in	the	charcoal	
industry.
In	the	first	year,	2019,	they	produced	5	000	tons	of	charcoal.		 From	2020	−	2022	the		
production	increased	with	1	500	tons	per	year	in	Namibia	and	Botswana.
The	following	information	is	available	from	Nam	Charcoal.

PENSAK  
Andrew	is	a	sole	trader	and	owns	a	business	called	Pensak.		The	business	specialises	
in	making	special	designed	pencil	bags/pouches,	marker	cases	and	pencil	cases.		The	
business	has	grown	quickly,	but	profits	stayed	the	same	over	the	last	two	years.		 A	
sudden	increase	in	demand	in	2024	forces	Andrew	to	change	the	working	hours	which	
put	the	workers	under	great	pressure	and	each	worker	gets	now	safety	instruction	that	
is	applicable	in	the	factory.		 Due	to	the	growth,	there	was	a	need	for	a	more	formal		
organisational	structure.		Andrew	make	use	of	worker	councils	and	quality	circles	as	a	way	
of	worker	participation	to	motivate	his	workforce.
Andrew	has	ten	skilled	workers	which	consist	of	two	store	workers,	three	shop	workers,	one	
cutter,	three	women	who	stitch	the	pencil	bags	on	sewing	machines,	as	well	as	a	receptionist.	 	 	
Workers	are	paid	by	piece	rate	but	they	didn’t	like	this	method.		Effective	communication	
and	safety	of	each	worker	is	vital	for	the	image	and	efficiency	of	Pensak.
Andrew	decide	to	give	his	workforce	more	responsibly,	recognition	for	their	good	work,	
promotion	and	growth	opportunities	in	the	work	place.		 This	will	lead	to	a	more	loyal	
workforce.
Andrew	wants	to	expand	the	business	and	decided	to	form	a	partnership 	with	his	
brother	Flip.
Currently	the	pencil	bags	are	promoted	through	advertising.		 Andrew	is	considering		
personal	selling	and	public	relations	to	make	schools	more	aware	of	his	products.
The	Namibian	government	plays	a	vital	role	in	the	economy	and	this	has	an	influence	on	
Pensak’s	business	activities	especially	the	customers.
The	following	information	was	taken	from	the	balance	sheet	of	Pensak	in	2024.

Current	liabilities N$57	000

Long-term	liabilities N$246	000
